units.title: Hello, I'm…
units.fact: Hamburg's harbor is Germany's gateway to the world; locals greet you with "Moin!" at any hour.

units.title: Who is who
units.fact: Lübeck, "Queen of the Hanseatic League", is famous for its marzipan and the brick Holstentor gate.

units.title: My family
units.fact: Kiel Week is the world's largest sailing event: millions come to the Baltic coast every June.

units.title: What I do
units.fact: The Town Musicians of Bremen (Grimm) — a donkey, dog, cat and rooster — stand bronze beside the town hall.

units.title: Questions
units.fact: Hannover's Herrenhausen Gardens are among Europe's finest Baroque gardens; its German is considered the most "standard".

units.title: At home
units.fact: Lüneburg grew rich on salt; its crooked brick houses lean because the ground beneath them was mined.

units.title: Food and drink
units.fact: Schwerin's fairy-tale castle sits on an island; the palace ghost "Petermännchen" is said to guard it.

units.title: Numbers and time
units.fact: Rostock's astronomical clock (1472) in St. Mary's Church still runs; its calendar disc was renewed in 2017 and now reaches to 2150.

units.title: Shopping
units.fact: Stralsund's Gothic brick churches and the Ozeaneum aquarium face the island of Rügen across the Strelasund.

units.title: Seasons by the sea
units.fact: Rügen's white chalk cliffs inspired Caspar David Friedrich's most famous painting.

units.title: Around the city
units.fact: Berlin has more bridges than Venice, and the little East German traffic-light man, the Ampelmännchen, became its mascot.

units.title: My things
units.fact: Frederick the Great's Sanssouci ("without worries") palace — he asked to be buried there beside his dogs.

units.title: Can, must, want
units.fact: Brandenburg an der Havel gave its name to the whole state; the Brandenburg Gate in Berlin was named after the road to it.

units.title: My day
units.fact: In the Spreewald, mail is delivered by boat along 1,300 km of canals — and the pickled gherkins are famous.

units.title: Do this!
units.fact: Cottbus is the center of the Lower Sorbs, a Slavic minority whose bilingual street signs and painted Easter eggs are unique in Germany.

units.title: Giving and helping
units.fact: Magdeburg's Hundertwasser "Green Citadel" has no straight lines — even the windows dance.

units.title: Getting around
units.fact: In 1517 Martin Luther posted his 95 Theses here; his German Bible shaped the language you are learning.

units.title: Where is it?
units.fact: The Bauhaus school (founded in Weimar, famous in Dessau) gave the world flat roofs, tubular-steel chairs and the idea that form follows function.

units.title: Work
units.fact: Handel was born in Halle; the city also has Germany's oldest chocolate factory (Halloren, 1804).

units.title: Review: the half-timbered town
units.fact: More than 1,300 half-timbered houses survive in Quedlinburg — a UNESCO town straight out of a fairy tale.

units.title: What I did
units.fact: Bach was cantor at Leipzig's St. Thomas Church for 27 years; the 1989 Monday demonstrations began here too.

units.title: Where I went
units.fact: Dresden's Frauenkirche was rebuilt stone by stone from the rubble of 1945 and reopened in 2005.

units.title: Made by hand
units.fact: Europe's first hard porcelain was made in Meißen in 1710 — look for the crossed blue swords.

units.title: I think that…
units.fact: Görlitz is so well preserved that Hollywood calls it "Görliwood" (The Grand Budapest Hotel was filmed here).

units.title: Because…
units.fact: A 7-meter bronze head of Karl Marx still dominates the center of Chemnitz, once called Karl-Marx-Stadt.

units.title: Describing people
units.fact: Goethe and Schiller lived in Weimar; their double statue stands outside the National Theatre.

units.title: Describing things
units.fact: Erfurt's Krämerbrücke is the longest inhabited bridge in Europe, lined with 32 houses.

units.title: Bigger, better, best
units.fact: Jena's Carl Zeiss works made the lenses that let astronomers see further than ever before.

units.title: Feelings
units.fact: Luther translated the New Testament in 11 weeks in the Wartburg castle above Eisenach, hiding as "Junker Jörg".

units.title: Review: castles and songs
units.fact: The Wartburg hosted the legendary minstrels' contest that inspired Wagner's Tannhäuser.

units.title: Once upon a time
units.fact: The Brothers Grimm collected their fairy tales in Kassel; the "Grimmwelt" museum is dedicated to them.

units.title: In the dark forest
units.fact: Marburg's university is the oldest Protestant one in the world; the Grimms studied law here.

units.title: Whose is it?
units.fact: Fulda grew around a monastery founded in 744; its cathedral holds the tomb of St. Boniface, "Apostle of the Germans".

units.title: Plans and the future
units.fact: Frankfurt's skyline earned it the nickname "Mainhattan"; Goethe was born here in 1749.

units.title: Science and inventions
units.fact: Darmstadt gave its name to element 110, darmstadtium, discovered at its heavy-ion research center.

units.title: Wine and festivals
units.fact: Würzburg's Residenz has the largest ceiling fresco in the world, painted by Tiepolo.

units.title: If only…
units.fact: Bamberg brews "Rauchbier" — smoked beer that tastes like bacon — and its old town is a UNESCO site.

units.title: Toys and Christmas
units.fact: Nürnberg's Christkindlesmarkt is one of the oldest Christmas markets; try the Lebkuchen and tiny Rostbratwürste.

units.title: In order to…
units.fact: Legend says Rothenburg was saved in 1631 when its mayor drank 3.25 liters of wine in one go — the "Meistertrunk".

units.title: Review: music and opera
units.fact: Wagner built his own opera house in Bayreuth; tickets for the festival can take years to get.

units.title: Before that…
units.fact: Cologne Cathedral took 632 years to finish; at carnival the city shouts "Kölle Alaaf!".

units.title: Memories
units.fact: Beethoven was born in Bonn in 1770; it was West Germany's capital from 1949 to 1990.

units.title: How things are made
units.fact: Düsseldorf's "Altbier" is dark, while Cologne's "Kölsch" is pale — never order one in the other city!

units.title: Emperors and history
units.fact: Charlemagne ruled his empire from Aachen; 31 German kings were crowned in its cathedral.

units.title: Industry and nature
units.fact: The Zollverein coal mine, once Europe's largest, is now a UNESCO site and design museum.

units.title: Bicycles and students
units.fact: Münster has more bicycles than inhabitants; the Peace of Westphalia was signed here in 1648.

units.title: Rivers and castles
units.fact: At the Deutsches Eck in Koblenz the Moselle flows into the Rhine beneath a giant statue of Wilhelm I.

units.title: Conversation tricks
units.fact: Gutenberg invented printing with movable type in Mainz around 1450.

units.title: He said that…
units.fact: Trier, founded by the Romans in 16 BC, is Germany's oldest city; the Porta Nigra gate is 1,800 years old.

units.title: Review: the wine river
units.fact: The Moselle's vineyards are among the steepest in the world, some at a 65° slope.

units.title: University life
units.fact: Heidelberg is Germany's oldest university town (1386); rowdy students were once locked in the Studentenkarzer.

units.title: Inventions
units.fact: Karl Benz built the first car in Mannheim; Bertha Benz made the first long road trip in it in 1888.

units.title: Engineering
units.fact: Stuttgart is home to both Mercedes-Benz and Porsche; the city's vineyards reach almost into the center.

units.title: Poets and thinkers
units.fact: The poet Hölderlin spent 36 years in a tower by Tübingen's river, cared for by a carpenter's family.

units.title: The green city
units.fact: Freiburg is one of Germany's sunniest cities and a pioneer of solar power; small streams called "Bächle" run through the streets.

units.title: Health and spa
units.fact: Baden-Baden's thermal baths have been used since Roman times; Mark Twain loved them.

units.title: The Black Forest
units.fact: The cuckoo clock and the Black Forest gâteau both come from here — and many of Grimm's darkest woods.

units.title: Lakes and borders
units.fact: Konstanz sits on Lake Constance where Germany, Austria and Switzerland meet with no agreed border in the water.

units.title: Records
units.fact: Ulm Minster has the tallest church steeple in the world (161.5 m); Einstein was born in Ulm.

units.title: Money and trade
units.fact: The Fuggerei in Augsburg, founded in 1516, is the oldest social housing in the world — rent is still under €1 a year.

units.title: In the beer garden
units.fact: Munich's Oktoberfest actually starts in September; the first one in 1810 celebrated a royal wedding.

units.title: Mountains and sport
units.fact: Germany's highest peak, the Zugspitze (2,962 m), towers over Garmisch-Partenkirchen.

units.title: The fairy-tale castle
units.fact: "Mad" King Ludwig II built Neuschwanstein near Füssen; Walt Disney modeled Sleeping Beauty's castle on it.

units.title: Medieval life
units.fact: Regensburg's Stone Bridge (1146) is one of the oldest in Germany; the sausage kitchen beside it has served since then.

units.title: Three rivers
units.fact: In Passau three rivers meet — the Danube, the Inn and the Ilz — each a different color.

units.title: Weddings and celebrations
units.fact: Every four years Landshut re-enacts a royal wedding of 1475 with 2,000 costumed citizens.

units.title: Weather and seasons
units.fact: On the Königssee near Berchtesgaden a boatman plays the trumpet so you can hear its echo come back from the cliffs again and again.

units.title: Emotions
units.fact: On an island in the Chiemsee Ludwig II built a copy of Versailles — and never finished it.

units.title: Careers
units.fact: Ingolstadt is where Mary Shelley's Victor Frankenstein studied and made his monster.

units.title: Theater and art
units.fact: Since 1634 the villagers of Oberammergau have staged a Passion Play every ten years, keeping a vow made during the plague.

units.title: Music
units.fact: Mozart was born in Salzburg in 1756; The Sound of Music was filmed all around the city.

units.title: Alpine life
units.fact: Innsbruck's "Golden Roof" is covered with 2,657 gilded copper tiles.

units.title: Small-town life
units.fact: Hallstatt is so picturesque that China built a full-scale copy of it.

units.title: Media and technology
units.fact: Linz's Ars Electronica festival has celebrated art and technology since 1979.

units.title: The coffee house
units.fact: In a Viennese café, a single coffee buys you the right to sit for hours with the newspapers.

units.title: Empire and history
units.fact: The Habsburgs ruled from Vienna for over 600 years; Schönbrunn Palace has 1,441 rooms.

units.title: Body and health
units.fact: Graz's clock tower has hands reversed: the big hand shows the hours.

units.title: Lakes and leisure
units.fact: Lake Wörthersee is warm enough for swimming into September.

units.title: Faith and monasteries
units.fact: The narrator of Umberto Eco's The Name of the Rose is Adso, a young monk from Melk Abbey.

units.title: Review: the floating stage
units.fact: Bregenz stages operas on a floating stage on Lake Constance for 7,000 spectators.

units.title: Banking and business
units.fact: Zürich's Bahnhofstrasse hides bank vaults under the pavement; the Swiss say "Grüezi".

units.title: Politics and society
units.fact: Einstein developed his theory of relativity while working in Bern's patent office.

units.title: Research
units.fact: Basel lies where Switzerland, Germany and France meet; it's a capital of chemistry and pharmaceuticals.

units.title: Legends
units.fact: Near Lake Lucerne William Tell is said to have shot the apple off his son's head.

units.title: Adventure and danger
units.fact: Between two lakes, Interlaken looks up at the Eiger, Mönch and Jungfrau.

units.title: Nature and animals
units.fact: Zermatt is car-free; the Matterhorn above it is one of the most photographed mountains on Earth.

units.title: Books and libraries
units.fact: St. Gallen's Abbey Library holds manuscripts over 1,200 years old; visitors wear felt slippers.

units.title: Law and order
units.fact: Liechtenstein, capital Vaduz, has more registered companies than citizens.

units.title: Home again
units.fact: Zeppelin airships were built on Lake Constance — you can still fly in one today.

units.title: The master's examination
units.fact: Your journeyman years are over: the guild examines your Meisterstück. Bestanden?
